message.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus faced opposition from the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic scholarly establishment, Lutheran preachers, and eventually elements of the Catholic Church. Johannes Stundt, a Lutheran pastor in Königsberg, publicly denounced his heliocentric theory in the 1540s. Many university professors considered the model unprovable and contrary to sensory experience. The Catholic Church did not formally condemn *De Revolutionibus* until the mid-seventeenth century, during the Galileo affair.

Who would dare challenge a cosmological framework that had stood for two thousand years? Why did so many respected scholars resist a model that contradicted what the naked eye seemed to show? Was it theology, philosophical commitment to Aristotelian physics, or simple intellectual inertia that fueled the resistance? How could a Polish canon lawyer's work be taken seriously by the broader European academic world?

How audacious it was to place the Earth in motion! What a formidable intellectual opposition Copernicus must have encountered throughout his career! It truly was a revolutionary act that reshaped all of natural philosophy. What a remarkable figure he was, even amid the controversy of his own lifetime!
